content: 1. Food Composition Data Sources: Food composition tables and databases from countries such as Colombia, France, Germany, India, Kenya, Korea, Malawi, Mali, Mexico, Nepal, New Zealand, Nigeria, Peru, Tanzania, Thailand, and Vietnam were utilized. These sources include national institutions, universities, and international organizations like FAO. Examples include the Colombian Food Composition Table (2018), the French Ciqual database (2020), the Indian Food Composition Tables (2017), and the Thai Food Composition Database (2018). 2. Methodology for Nutrient Profile Development: Draft nutrient profiles were reviewed to identify and address outliers within food subgroups. This involved examining the range of nutrient values, the difference between mean and median values, and the impact of excluding extreme outliers. Adjustments were made conservatively, ensuring that outliers were only excluded or replaced when they had a significant impact on the mean or were deemed unreliable. In some cases, items were excluded or nutrient values were set to missing. 3. Refinement of Food Subgroups: Certain food subgroups were narrowed for modeling purposes. For example, liver was modeled separately due to its consistently high vitamin A content compared to other organ meats. Similarly, seafood was excluded in favor of fish due to its high nutrient variability and lower consumption rates. 4. Nutrient Density Calculations: Nutrient densities (per 1000 kcal) were calculated for macronutrients, fiber, and micronutrients. 5. Single Staple Food Patterns: Nutrient profiles were modeled for three types of staple food patterns: rice-based, maize-based, and root/tuber-based diets. For rice, the most common type reported (white, long-grain, unenriched) was selected. For maize, whole-grain white maize flour was chosen, while root and tuber profiles represented cooked forms. 6. Sentinel Unhealthy Foods and Fortified Items: Nutrient profiles for unhealthy foods and fortified items were calculated as unweighted averages. Fortified items included micronutrient powders and lipid-based nutrient supplements. 7. Country-Specific Food Items: The number of food items reported for infants and young children varied by country, with France reporting the highest (100 items) and Zambia the lowest (19 items). Food items were grouped into categories such as starchy staples, fruits, vegetables, dairy, meat, fish, and oils. 8. Food Group and Subgroup Analysis: Detailed nutrient values were provided for various food groups, including whole grains, refined grains, starchy roots, vitamin A-rich fruits and vegetables, legumes, nuts, seeds, dairy, eggs, meat, fish, and oils. Each subgroup was analyzed for its nutrient content, with adjustments made for raw, cooked, or processed forms. 9. Outlier Management: Outliers were addressed by replacing nutrient values with alternative data, setting values to missing, or excluding items entirely. High heterogeneity within subgroups was acknowledged and, in some cases, led to further division of subgroups. 10. Nutrient Profiles for Non-Target Nutrients: Profiles for vitamins and fatty acids were calculated, with adjustments made for missing data. For example, niacin equivalents were calculated using available data for niacin and tryptophan, while fatty acid values were supplemented with undifferentiated data when specific values were unavailable. 11. Modeling and Data Representation: Nutrient profiles were weighted based on the number of countries reporting consumption of a given food item. Data from 38 countries were included, and the number of food items per country was documented.
